headline: Thunder was originally “god” + “cry out”: 神 (kami) + 鳴り (nari).

sources.quote: Originally a compound of 神(かみ) (kami, “god, spirit”) + 鳴(な)り (nari, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 鳴(な)る (naru, “to cry out, to call”)).

quotes: /kaminari/ → /kamʉnari/ → /kanːari/
Shift in pronunciation from kaminari above.
⟨ika tu ti⟩ → ⟨ikaduti⟩ → /ikad͡zut͡ɕi/ → /ikazut͡ɕi/
From Old Japanese.
Originally a compound of 厳(いか) (ika, “sternness, terribleness, imposingness”) + つ (tsu, Old Japanese possessive particle) + 霊(ち) (chi, “spirit, force, essence”).
Compound of 鳴(な)る (naru, “to cry out, to call”) + 神(かみ) (kami, “god, spirit”).
From Middle Chinese 雷 (MC lwoj).
Compare modern Mandarin 雷 (léi) and Cantonese 雷 (leoi⁴).

examples.en: The heavy rain was accompanied with thunder.

headline: The rainbow may once have been nuji or noji: the source suggests a shift from those earlier readings.

sources.quote: ⟨nizi⟩ → /niʑi/
From Old Japanese 虹 (nizi), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *nonsi. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Also attested as man’yōgana form 爾自 in the 金光明最勝王経音義 (Konkōmyō Saishōō-kyō Ongi) of 1079. May be a shift from earlier ぬじ (nuji) or のじ (noji) readings.

quotes: From Middle Chinese 虹 (MC huwng).

examples.en: A rainbow is a natural phenomenon.

headline: Many theories for “rice”, from “doing with one's heart” to Austronesian cousins — the last called extremely speculative.

sources.quote: ⟨ko₂me₂⟩ → */kəməj/ → /kome/
From Old Japanese. First appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 渠(こ)梅(め). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *kəmay.
Many theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation:

* Perhaps from 籠(こ)め (kome), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 籠(こ)める (komeru, “to do with one's heart”)., from the way rice is farmed. The accent of kome in the Heian period is , while kome- in the Heian period is .
* Possibly cognate with Proto-Vietic *kəːm (“cooked rice”), modern cơm.

* Possibly cognate with Proto-Austronesian *Semay and Old Chinese 糜 (OC *mral). However, this is extremely speculative; none of the known derivations from Proto-Austronesian *Semay develop initial /k/, nor is this shift explainable by any known mechanism within Japonic.

quotes: ⟨yo₂nai⟩ → */jənai/ → */jəne/ → /jone/
First attested in the Wamyō Ruijushō (938 CE).
From Proto-Japonic *yənəi; possibly related to 稲 (ine, “rice plant”).
The colloquial sense is derived from the components of the 米 kanji: 八 (hachi, “eight”) + 十 (jū, “ten”) + 八 (hachi, “eight”).
Probably a shortened reduplication of kome (see above).
First cited to a work from 1275.
From Middle Chinese 米 (MC mejX).

examples.ja: 父は米を栽培している。
日本では米が主食です。
examples.en: The main diet in Japan is rice.

headline: Three theories for sake — “flourish”, “ward off” cold illness, or a corruption of kushi — and none is settled.

sources.quote: ⟨sake₂⟩ → /sakəɨ/ → /sake/

From Old Japanese 酒 (sake₂), from Proto-Japonic *sakai. Cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *sake. Attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, with the ideographic spelling 酒. Additionally, appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE and the Man'yōshū of c. 759 CE. This is the standalone form of saka- below.
Various theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation:
* Might be cognate with 栄(さか)え (sakae), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 栄(さか)える (sakaeru, “to flourish”).
* Might be derived from 避(さ)ける (sakeru, “to ward off, to shun”), from the idea that drinking alcohol would ward off cold diseases.
* Might be derived from or a corruption of 酒(くし) (kushi, “rice wine, rice vodka, sake”); however, the phonological shifts required are completely unexplainable.
* The final -ke may be an apophonic form of Old Japanese 酒 (ki₁).

quotes: From Old Japanese 酒 (saka). Likely the original form of sake above. Rarely used in isolation. Mostly used as the first element in compounds.

Originally a 女(にょう)房(ぼう)詞(ことば) (nyōbō kotoba, literally “women's word”) term, possibly derived from reduplication of the first syllable sa from sake. Alternately, may be derived by metaphor from the Chinese-derived euphemism for sake, 竹(ちく)葉(よう) (chikuyō, literally “bamboo leaves”), as 笹(ささ) (sasa) refers to a type of short, leafy bamboo.
From Middle Chinese 酒 (MC tsjuwX).

examples.en: Don't indulge yourself too much in drinking.
Let's have a drink or something.

headline: A pot named for a snack: 鍋 is na (“small snack”) + he (“pot”), with rendaku turning he into be.

sources.quote: ⟨nabe₂⟩ → */naⁿbe/ → /nabe/
From Old Japanese, first cited in the Nihon Shoki of 720. In turn, reconstructed as Proto-Japonic *nanpay.

Originally a compound of Old Japanese elements 肴 (na, “small snack, hors d'oeuvre”) + 瓮 (pe, modern he, “a pot or pan for holding food or beverages”). The he changes to be as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

examples.en: Don't let the pan boil dry.

examples.ja: 鍋がふきこぼれているよ。
furigana: がふきこぼれているよ。

headline: Shio is cognate with Ainu sippo, and the Nippo Jisho of 1603 shows it already softened.

sources.quote: ⟨sipo⟩ → /ɕiɸo/ → /ɕiwo/ → /ɕio/
From Old Japanese, cited in the Kojiki of 712 CE. The Old Japanese term is cognate to Ainu シㇷ゚ポ (sippo) and Ainu シㇱポ (sispo).
Cognate with 潮 (shio, “[ocean] tide”).
The medial consonant had already lenited to /w/ by 1603, as recorded in the Nippo Jisho.

quotes: From Middle Chinese 鹽 (MC yem, “salt”) and 鹽 (MC yemH, “to salt; salting”).

examples.ja: このスープは塩が少し足りない。
examples.en: This soup wants a bit of salt.

headline: Vovin considers miso a borrowing from Koreanic — compare meju — and a 938 source calls it a “Korean sauce”.

sources.quote: ⟨mi₁so₁⟩ → /miso/
From Old Japanese. First attested in Ritsuryō tax records from 738 CE, with the spelling 未醤.

Possibly also attested with the spelling 末醤 on a mokkan (wooden tally stick) dated to the reign of Emperor Junnin during the years 758–764, although this might be a different word, as 未 and 末 are distinct characters with separate pronunciations and opposite meanings.
Phonetically recorded as 美蘇 in the Wamyō Ruijushō of 938, but the commentary describes this as erroneously written as 未醤.

Vovin considers it to be a borrowing from Koreanic, compare Modern Korean 메주 (meju) "brick of dried fermented soybeans." This is supported by the Ruijushō citing the Youshikangosho saying that it is a "Korean sauce".
Cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *miso. A Proto-Japonic *misV is sometimes reconstructed as the ancestor for both if Ryukyuan didn't borrow it directly from Japanese.

headline: An egg is a “ball child”: 玉 (tama) + 子 (ko), with ko voiced to go.

sources.quote: From 玉 (tama, “ball”) + 子 (ko, “child, small thing”). The ko reading for 子 changes to go as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

quotes: From Middle Chinese 卵 (MC lwanX).

headline: Japanese for “pencil” is a calque of English “lead pencil”, built from a Chinese word.

sources.quote: Calque of English lead pencil, from Middle Chinese 鉛筆 (MC ywen pit)

examples.ja: えんぴつであなたの名前を書きなさい。
examples.en: Write your name with the pencil.

examples.ja: 少年はエンピツをとがらせておくのが好きだった。
examples.en: The boy liked to keep his pencils sharp.
furigana: はエンピツをとがらせておくのが

headline: Fuyu began with a p: Old Japanese puyu, from Proto-Japonic *puyu.

sources.quote: ⟨puyu⟩ → /ɸuju/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *puyu.

quotes: From Middle Chinese 冬 (MC towng).

examples.en: I feel more tired in the wintertime.

headline: Samui was samushi, and from the Muromachi period it was sometimes pronounced sabushi.

sources.quote: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 寒(さむ)し (samushi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i).

Starting in at least the Muromachi period, this term became sporadically pronounced with a medial /b/ as 寒(さぶ)し (sabushi) (not to be confused with 寂(さぶ)し (sabushi), original form of 寂(さび)しい (sabishii)). Compare the similar /m/~/b/ alternation seen in 寂しい (sabishii, samishii, “lonely, desolate”), 頭 (tsuburi, tsumuri, “head”), and 煙 (keburi, kemuri, “smoke”). Related to 冷(さ)む (samu, “to cool down”), modern 冷(さ)める (sameru).

examples.ja: 寒いからコートを着るべきだ。
examples.en: It's cold so you should wear a coat.

examples.ja: 昨夜はすごく寒かったから、外に出ないで中に閉じこもってたよ。
examples.en: It was very cold last night, so we didn't go outside, but stayed indoors.

headline: Snow is yuki, but one eastern-dialect song in the Man'yōshū has yoki, and some reconstruct *yoki as the ancestor.

sources.quote: ⟨yuki₁⟩ → */jukʲi/ → /juki/
From Old Japanese. Found in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.
Also found once in the Man'yōshū in a so-called 東歌 (Azuma uta, literally “eastern song”) in the eastern dialect of Old Japanese, realized as ⟨yo₂ki₁⟩.
Reconstructed by some as deriving from Proto-Japonic *yoki.

headline: Ice is a verb turned noun: kōri is the stem of 凍る (kōru, “to freeze”).

sources.quote: ⟨ko₂pori⟩ → */kəpori/ → /koɸori/ → /kowori/ → /koːri/
From Old Japanese.
The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 凍(こお)る (kōru, “to freeze”).

quotes: ⟨pi₁⟩ → */pʲi/ → /ɸi/ → /hi/
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Man'yōshū of circa 759 CE.
Possibly cognate with 冷える (hieru, “to become cold”).
Compare Middle Chinese 冰 (MC ping).
From Middle Chinese 冰 (MC ping).

headline: Smoke was keburi before it was kemuri, and the shorter kemu is a clipping attested since 1275.

sources.quote: /keburi/ → /kemuri/
Shift from Old Japanese-derived keburi reading (see below) as a regular /b/ → /m/ change. Appears in the Taiheiki of the late 1300s.
Now the most common reading.
/kemuri/ → /kemu/
Clipping of earlier kemuri.
Attested since at least 1275.

quotes: The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 煙る (keburu, “to be smoky, to give off smoke”). Appears with this reading in the Man'yōshū.
Clipping of earlier keburi.
From Middle Chinese 煙 (MC 'en).

examples.ja: 彼は部屋に満ちていた煙にむせ返った。
examples.en: He was choked by the smoke which filled the room.

examples.ja: 仕事している時に他人のたばこのけむりを吸うのはいやだ。
examples.en: I don't like to inhale someone's smoke while I'm working.

headline: Fire has a hidden twin: hi is an apophonic form of ho, as ki (“tree”) pairs with ko-.

sources.quote: ⟨pi₂⟩ → */pʷɨ/ → /ɸi/ → /hi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *poy.
Apophonic form of ho (see below). Compare 木 (ki, ko-, “tree”).

quotes: /po/ → /ɸo/ → /ho/
From Old Japanese.
Combining form of hi above. Probably the oldest form, possibly cognate with Korean 불 (bul, “fire”).
/kwa/ → /ka/
From Middle Chinese 火 (MC xwaX).

headline: Flame is “fire's ear of grain”: 火 (ho) + の (no) + 穂 (ho).

sources.quote: ⟨po no₂ po⟩ → */ponəpo/ → /ɸonoɸo/ → /ɸonowo/ → /honowo/ → /hono.o/
From Old Japanese 炎 (pono₂po).
Compound of 火 (ho, combining form of hi, “fire”) + の (no, possessive particle) + 穂 (ho, “ear (of grain)”).

quotes: Compound of 火 (ho, “fire”, combining form) + 群 (mura, “gathering, group”).
/emʉ/ → /eɴ/
From Middle Chinese 炎 (MC hjem).
炎 is a daiyōji replacing 焔.

headline: Yu goes back to Proto-Japonic *yu and appears in both the Kojiki (712 CE) and the Man'yōshū.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *yu.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. Also used in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.

quotes: Baby talk. Possibly onomatopoeic of a person blowing on a hot beverage.

examples.ja: 砂糖は湯に入れると溶ける。
この湯は精神と肉体の調和をもたらすと言われています。
examples.en: It is said that this hot water brings a balance between body and mind.

headline: Japanese ストーブ is borrowed straight from English stove.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English stove.

examples.ja: 彼はストーブで体を暖めた。
examples.en: He warmed himself at the stove.

examples.ja: ストーブで体を温めなさい。

headline: Japanese セーター is borrowed straight from English sweater.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English sweater.

examples.ja: 彼女はセーターを着た。
このセーターは暖かい。

headline: Who borrowed from whom? Some Japanese sources say kutsu comes from Korean gudu; some Korean sources say the reverse.

sources.quote: ⟨kutu⟩: */kutu/ → /kut͡su/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kutu. Cognate with Yaeyama 草鞋 (futsï), Yonaguni 草鞋 (c'i).
Found in the Man'yōshū poetry compilation, completed circa 759.

Ultimate derivation unclear. Some Japanese sources suggest a borrowing from or cognate with Korean 구두 (gudu, “shoes”), but then some Korean sources suggest that the Korean term was borrowed from Japanese 靴 (kutsu, “shoes”).

headline: A cough is a verb stem, and seki is cognate with 堰 (seki, “dam”).

sources.quote: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb せく (seku, “to cough”). Cognate with 堰 (seki, “dam”).

headline: House took four steps from ipe to ie, and Old Korean may have a cousin.

sources.quote: ⟨ipe₁⟩ → /ipʲe/ → /iɸe/ → /iwe/ → /ie/
From Old Japanese. Possibly cognate with Old Korean 邑勒 (iprʌk, “house”).
Possibly related to 廬 (iho → io, “temporary hut”).

quotes: Inherited from Old Japanese [Term?], from Proto-Japonic *utui.
Doublet of 内(うち) (uchi, “middle, inside”).
Contraction of uchi above.
Often following the genitive case marker の (no) which contracts to -n.
From Middle Chinese 家 (MC kae).
The 漢音 (kan'on, literally “Han sound”), so likely a latter borrowing from Middle Chinese.
From Middle Chinese 家 (MC kae).
The 呉音 (goon, literally “Wu sound”), so likely the initial borrowing from Middle Chinese.

headline: A wall is a “place divider”: 処 (ka, “place”) + 重 (he, “division”), with he voiced to be.

sources.quote: Compound of 処(か) (ka, “place”) + 重(へ) (he, “division”), in reference to walls dividing objects apart. The he changes to be as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

examples.ja: 彼は壁にペンキの上塗りをした。
examples.en: He put the final coat of paint on the wall.

examples.ja: かべにかかっている絵をごらんなさい。
examples.en: Look at the picture on the wall.

headline: Yuka meant “bed” in the Nihon Shoki, and a 1668 scholar derived it from “not going”.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Attested in the 日(に)本(ほん)書(しょ)紀(き) (Nihon Shoki), completed in 720 and one of the earliest works written in Japanese, with a meaning of “bed”.

According to the 和(わ)句(く)解(げ) (Wakuge), published in 1668 by early Edo-period scholar 松(まつ)永(なが)貞(てい)徳(とく) (Matsunaga Teitoku), derives from 行(ゆ)か (yuka), the 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) stem of the verb 行(ゆ)く (yuku, “to go”), of an original meaning similar to “not going”, in reference to a place where one sits down to rest.

quotes: ⟨to₂ko₂⟩ → /toko/
From Old Japanese. Cognate with 所 (tokoro, “place”). Attested since at least the Nara period, appearing in the Man'yōshū, completed in 759.

Possibly an ancient compound of ⟨to₁⟩ (Proto-Japonic *to (“place”), as in 跡 ⟨ato₁⟩, “footprint, track”, from “foot place, where one has stepped”) + ⟨ko₂⟩ (noun-forming suffixing element denoting “place”, as in ここ ⟨ko₂ko₂⟩, “here”, from “this place”).
/ʑau/ → /ɕau/ → /ɕɔː/ → /ɕoː/
From Middle Chinese 床 (MC dzrjang). Devoicing apparently occurred after borrowing.

headline: Mise is short for misedana: miseru (“to show”) + tana (“shelf”).

sources.quote: Short for earlier 見(み)せ棚(だな) (misedana), from 見(み)せる (miseru, “to show”) + 棚(たな) (tana, “shelf”).

quotes: From Middle Chinese 店 (MC temH).

headline: A mirror is “shadow-seeing”: kaga (影, “shadow; image”) + mi (見, “seeing”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kankami.

Originally a compound of 影 (kaga, ancient combining form of 影 (kage), “shadow; outline; figure; image”) + 見 (mi, “seeing”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 見る (miru), “to see, to look at”).

quotes: /kjau/ → /kjɔː/ → /kjoː/
From Middle Chinese 鏡 (MC kjaengH).

examples.en: The eye is the mirror of the soul.

headline: Hoshi began as posi, from Proto-Japonic *pəsi.

sources.quote: /posi/ → /ɸoɕi/ → /hoɕi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pəsi.

quotes: From Middle Chinese 星 (MC seng).
The Singapore sense derives from the pre-World War Two kanji spelling 星加坡 (modern kanji spelling 新加坡) as borrowed from Chinese, itself a transliteration of Malay Singapura.

examples.en: Let me wish upon a shooting star.

headline: Tsuki was once tuki, and Wiktionary notes a vowel alternation between its standalone and combining forms.

sources.quote: ⟨tuki₂⟩ → */tukɨ/ → */t͡sukɨ/ → /t͡suki/
From Old Japanese 月 (tuki₂), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tukui.
For the vowel alternation, see WT:AJPX#Standalone forms and combining forms.

quotes: /ɡʷatɨ/ → /ɡʷat͡su/ → /ɡat͡su/
From Middle Chinese 月 (ŋʉɐt̚).
/ɡʷetu/ → /ɡet͡su/
From Middle Chinese 月 (ŋʉɐt̚).
Compare modern Hakka 月 (ngie̍t), Min Nan 月 (ge̍h).
/ɡʷat͡ɕi/ → /ɡat͡ɕi/
First attested in the Edo period.

Appears to be a poetic use of the 呉(ご)音(おん) (goon, literally “Wu sound”) reading, in reference to a rank of 端(はし)女(じょ)郎(ろう) (hashi jorō, “low-end prostitute]”) in the Kansai region. According to a popular song, a 月(がち) (gachi, “moon”) prostitute cost one 匁(もんめ) (monme, old unit of currency, worth roughly 3.75 grams of silver), a 影(かげ) (kage, “shadow”) prostitute cost two monme, and a 汐(しお) (shio, “tide; loveliness”) prostitute cost three monme.
Either a shift in sense from the low-ranking prostitute meaning above, or a shift in pronunciation from 頑(がん)痴(ち) (ganchi, literally “stubborn and stupid”).

headline: One dictionary says neko is a shortening of nekoma, but neko is attested in 794 and nekoma only in 918.

sources.quote: ⟨neko₁⟩ → /neko/
From Old Japanese. Cognate with Miyako にか (nika, “cat”, Tarama and Minna dialects) via unknown Japonic substratum.

Listed in modern references as a compound of ね (ne, onomatopoeia of the sound a cat makes; compare modern Japanese にゃ (nya), English mew, meow) + こ (ko, diminutive noun-forming suffix). According to the 和(わ)名(みょう)類(るい)聚(じゅ)抄(しょう) (Wamyō Ruijushō) of 931–938, neko is a shortening of 猫(ねこま) (nekoma), but neko appears in texts earlier than nekoma: neko is first attested in the Shin'yaku Kegonkyō Ongi Shiki of 794, while nekoma is not attested until 918 in the 本(ほん)草(ぞう)和(わ)名(みょう) (Honzō Wamyō, the oldest surviving dictionary of medicine in Japan).
A comparison of accent patterns between the dialects shows some confusion (see dialectal data):

* One group of dialects behaves as if was the Heian Kyoto accent pattern: many dialects with the Tokyo type accent, including the standard Japanese in Tokyo, pronounce this word with an pitch pattern, and in some non-mainstream Keihan type dialects as well, this word has a corresponding pitch pattern.

* Another group of dialects behaves as if was the Heian Kyoto accent pattern: the mainstream Keihan type dialects pronounce this word with an pitch pattern, and in a few of the Tokyo type dialects, this word has a corresponding pitch pattern.

As a result, this term is one example of words that have the same pitch accent pattern between Tokyo and Osaka/Kyoto. The confusion seems to be due to an impression that the term comes from a compound word origin.

quotes: According to the 和(わ)名(みょう)類(るい)聚(じゅ)抄(しょう) (Wamyō Ruijushō) of 931–938, the term 猫(ねこ) (neko) is a shortening of nekoma.
猫: 野王案、猫、音苗、禰古麻、下總本有和名二字興河海抄引此合、本草和名同訓、或省云禰古、新撰字鏡、狸、禰古、按狸一名猫、見本草和名、似虎而小、熊捕鼠為糧

Cat. According to Yewang, cat, sound-reading myō, [Japanese reading] nekoma; later compendia have a two character Japanese name - perhaps the Rivers and Seas Annotations references this compilation, the Honzō wamyō [has] a kun homophone, certain omissions call it 'neko', [in the] Shinsen Jikyō 'tanuki' - [read] neko, to check 'tanuki' [as] one name [for] a cat - see the Honzō wamyō; like a tiger but small, the creature catches rats for food

However, nekoma is first cited to 918 in the 本(ほん)草(ぞう)和(わ)名(みょう) (Honzō Wamyō, the oldest surviving dictionary of medicine in Japan), while 猫(ねこ) (neko) is first attested earlier in the Shin'yaku Kegonkyō Ongi Shiki of 794.
家狸、一名猫、和名禰古末
A house raccoon; also called a cat; the Japanese name is nekoma.

One theory about the derivation describes the first mora ⟨ne⟩ as onomatopoeia for the sound a cat makes, compare modern Japanese にゃ (nya), English mew, meow. The last two morae ⟨ko₁ma⟩ might accord with 熊(くま) (kuma, “bear”) if it were from Proto-Japonic *koma (class 2.3 ), in the sense of "four-legged animal". However, Japanese kuma appears to have cognates in ancient Koreanic sources meaning specifically "bear" (see the 熊(くま) (kuma, “bear”) entry for further details), making this theory less likely.

The Heian Kyoto accent of this word is ; note that in compound words for species names, the pitch pattern may be simplified to <-HL> when the final element is a 2-mora noun (e.g. 青(あお)海(の)苔(り) (aonori ← àwònórì ← *àwò-nòrì, “green laver”), and the presence or absence of this phenomenon could explain the accent confusion in neko.

headline: Derivation uncertain: from “to leave”, from “house” + “sleep”, from 狗 — or borrowed from some unknown language.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *enu. Derivation uncertain. Various theories exist, including derivation from ancient verb 往ぬ (inu, “to leave, to be gone”), from the way a dog will guard the house while the master is away; from a compound of 家 (ie, “house, home”) + 寝 (nu, “to sleep”, ancient monosyllabic form of modern 寝る neru); from ancient Japanese 狗 (enu < wenu, “puppy, dog”), itself of uncertain derivation; or as a borrowing from some other unknown language.

examples.ja: これらのイヌは大きい。
いぬが後についてきた。
